title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Business Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: From Indianapolis Apothecary to the Incretin Age

epigraph.quote: Take what you find here and make it better and better.
epigraph.author: Colonel Eli Lilly, Founder (1876)

web_blocks.html: Colonel Eli Lilly founded Eli Lilly and Company in May 1876 in Indianapolis, Indiana. He was a chemist and Union veteran tired of weak, uneven patent tonics. Instead of selling cures straight to buyers, he sold tested drugs only through doctors. By the 1880s, his firm sold gelatin-coated pills, fruit syrups, and lab-tested batches. That early rule still drives the firm today. When Lilly pairs hard biology with top plant scale, it compounds for decades. When it leans on one patent without a deep pipeline, it hits steep sales cliffs.

The first big shift came in 1923 with Iletin, the first mass-made insulin. Lilly teamed up with Toronto scientists Frederick Banting and Charles Best to scale it. Moving insulin from a lab bench to national supply meant solving purity, cold storage, and batch strength. Those skills made Lilly the top U.S. diabetes firm for a century. In 1982, Lilly repeated that feat with Humulin, the first human insulin made with DNA tech alongside Genentech. Lilly willingly replaced its own animal insulin before rivals could.

From 1987 to 2010, Lilly shifted toward brain and primary-care drugs. The 1987 launch of Prozac (fluoxetine), the first SSRI pill, changed depression care and powered growth through the 1990s. When Prozac lost U.S. patent protection in 2001, Lilly bridged the gap with Zyprexa (1996) and Cymbalta (2004). Yet leaning on small-molecule brain drugs set up the worst drop in modern company history. In the 2011–2014 'YZ' cliff, Zyprexa (2011) and Cymbalta (2013) lost U.S. patents within 26 months. That shock wiped out over $8 billion in high-margin sales and forced deep cuts.

web_blocks.takeaway: Lilly's 150-year history shows that enduring value creation has always come from solving complex biology plus industrial manufacturing—first with Iletin and Humulin, and now with tirzepatide, Foundayo, and retatrutide.

web_blocks.html: Lilly planted the seeds of its current rise during the 2011–2014 patent cliff. Under John Lechleiter and then CEO David A. Ricks (who took over in January 2017), Lilly exited crowded primary-care lines and spun off Elanco Animal Health in 2018–2019. Management focused R&D on four core areas: metabolic care, cancer, immune disease, and brain health. Lilly's chemists also refused to stop at single GLP-1 drugs, where Novo Nordisk led early. Instead, they built tirzepatide, a single peptide that targets both GIP and GLP-1 receptors.

Approved as Mounjaro for diabetes in May 2022 and Zepbound for obesity in November 2023, tirzepatide beat older GLP-1 drugs on both blood sugar and weight loss (over 20% in SURMOUNT-1). It sparked the fastest sales ramp in drug history. Combined Mounjaro and Zepbound sales hit $36.5 billion in FY2025, or 56% of Lilly's $65,179 million total, and topped $16 billion in Q3 2026 alone. Lilly also licensed oral small-molecule orforglipron from Chugai, winning FDA approval as Foundayo on April 1, 2026. Meanwhile, triple-agonist retatrutide cleared Phase 3 TRIUMPH trials ahead of a Q1 2027 filing.

web_blocks.title: Base-Rate Warning: Pfizer's 2011 Lipitor Cliff & Exubera Write-Off (2006–2015)
web_blocks.summary: Pharmaceutical history is littered with mega-blockbusters that masked underlying R&D productivity decay and delivery miscalculations. When Pfizer's atorvastatin (Lipitor) approached its November 2011 U.S. patent expiration after peaking near $13 billion in annual sales, management attempted to bridge the gap with Exubera, an inhaled insulin launched in 2006 that required bulky inhaler devices and pulmonary monitoring. Patients and physicians rejected the delivery friction, forcing Pfizer to write off $2.8 billion in 2007 and endure a multi-year revenue contraction post-2011.
lessons: Single-molecule dominance creates organizational complacency unless next-generation modalities (like oral small-molecule Foundayo and triple-agonist retatrutide) are commercialized years before patent expiry.

Delivery convenience and manufacturing economics matter as much as molecular efficacy: injectable-only bottlenecks invite compounding leakage, whereas oral small-molecule scale solves both cold-chain and patient friction.
Mega-cap pharma acquisitions rarely replace organic R&D engines; Lilly's disciplined internal + targeted bolt-on model (e.g., Loxo Oncology, Chugai licensing) avoided value-destructive mega-mergers.

web_blocks.title: Price-Blind Historical Takeaway
paragraphs: Lilly has survived three major patent cliffs over the past 25 years (Prozac in 2001, Zyprexa in 2011, Cymbalta in 2013) and emerged with a broader, more durable biologics and peptide/small-molecule platform each time. The central business question entering 2027 is whether Lilly can convert today's tirzepatide cash gusher into a multi-decade cardiometabolic, oncology, immunology, and neuroscience franchise before payer price compression and eventual 2036+ patent expirations arrive.

web_blocks.html: From 2017 to 2026, Lilly paired internal lab work with focused deal-making. Unlike peers that chased giant, debt-heavy mergers (such as Pfizer-Wyeth or BMS-Celgene), Lilly stuck to $1 billion to $8 billion bolt-on deals. Loxo Oncology ($8 billion in 2019) added cancer drugs Retevmo and Jaypirca, while Dermira (2020) brought Ebglyss. Avid and Prevail boosted brain imaging and gene therapy. Chugai's 2018 orforglipron license later became Foundayo in April 2026.

Just as key, Lilly cut legacy clutter. Spinning off Elanco in 2018–2019 and letting older primary-care drugs fade kept R&D output among the best in big pharma. By 2025, six drugs—Mounjaro, Zepbound, Verzenio, Trulicity, Taltz, and Jardiance—each topped $3 billion in yearly sales. Newer launches Kisunla, Ebglyss, Omvoh, and Jaypirca also began scaling toward multi-hundred-million-dollar run-rates.

book_paragraphs: If you and I want to understand why Eli Lilly operates with a distinct institutional rhythm compared to serial acquirers in global pharmaceuticals, we have to start in May 1876 on a quiet street in Indianapolis. Colonel Eli Lilly, a Union artillery officer and trained pharmacist, was disgusted by the patent-medicine peddlers of his day—elixirs that promised miracle cures with zero batch consistency. He built a company around a radical premise for the 1870s: sell only through physicians, assay every batch scientifically, and never stop improving the formulation. That founding ethos—captured in his famous charge to his son, 'Take what you find here and make it better and better'—still governs how the firm allocates R&D capital a century and a half later.

Every great industrial franchise has an origin story where science meets manufacturing scale, and for Lilly that moment arrived in 1923. When Frederick Banting and Charles Best discovered insulin in Toronto, they could barely produce enough extract to keep a handful of patients alive. Lilly's chemists solved the industrial purification and stabilization problem, launching Iletin and turning a fragile academic breakthrough into a reliable, nationwide medicine. Nearly sixty years later, in 1982, Lilly did it again with Humulin, partnering with Genentech to bring the first recombinant DNA human insulin to market—willingly obsoleting its own animal-insulin cash cow before a competitor could.

To understand why that matters, think about what happens to most hundred-year-old pharmaceutical companies when their flagship patents expire. Management teams panic. They hire investment bankers, borrow thirty or fifty billion dollars to buy a rival with an aging pipeline, promise Wall Street two billion dollars in cost synergies, and spend the next five years laying off scientists while their R&D labs wither. Lilly did the exact opposite during its 2011–2014 'YZ' patent cliff.

Under John Lechleiter and then Dave Ricks, Lilly accepted several years of flat revenue around $20 billion to $22 billion so it could protect its internal R&D engine at 23% to 25% of sales. Instead of buying scale, Lilly bought targeted scientific capabilities: Loxo Oncology for precision kinase inhibitors like Jaypirca, Dermira for Ebglyss in atopic dermatitis, and a quiet 2018 licensing agreement with Japan's Chugai Pharmaceutical for an oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonist called orforglipron. At the time, almost nobody on Wall Street cared about a preclinical Chugai small molecule. Eight years later, on April 1, 2026, that molecule became Foundayo—the first oral non-peptide GLP-1 approved for weight management without food or water restrictions.

book_subsections.title: The Painful Lessons of the 'YZ' Patent Cliff
paragraphs: You cannot appreciate the discipline of Lilly's modern leadership without studying the scar tissue from 2011 to 2014. In the 1990s and 2000s, Lilly rode a wave of small-molecule central nervous system blockbusters—first Prozac in depression, then Zyprexa in schizophrenia, then Cymbalta in depression and pain. They were extraordinary medicines, and they generated torrential cash flows. But when Zyprexa lost U.S. patent protection in 2011 and Cymbalta followed in 2013, generic competition erased billions of dollars of high-margin revenue almost overnight. For nearly six years, Lilly's top line stagnated around $20 billion to $22 billion while R&D budgets were stretched thin.

Instead of panicking into a mega-merger—the classic big-pharma reflex that destroys culture and R&D productivity—Lilly's board promoted David A. Ricks to CEO in January 2017. Ricks and his scientific leadership made a contrarian bet: divest the non-core Elanco Animal Health business, exit crowded primary-care categories, and double down on four high-unmet-need pillars where biology was finally driving disease modification—cardiometabolic disease, oncology, immunology, and neuroscience.

book_subsections.title: From GLP-1 Challenger to Incretin Architect
paragraphs: At the time Ricks took over, Novo Nordisk already held the lead in GLP-1 receptor agonists. Rather than launching a me-too GLP-1, Lilly's peptide chemists hypothesized that co-activating two gut hormone receptors—GIP and GLP-1—in a single molecule could deliver deeper metabolic reset without proportionally worse gastrointestinal side effects. That hypothesis became tirzepatide. Approved as Mounjaro for Type 2 diabetes in May 2022 and Zepbound for obesity in November 2023, tirzepatide didn't just take share; it expanded the entire addressable market, driving $36.5 billion in combined FY2025 sales and over $16 billion in Q3 2026 alone.

Even more telling is what Lilly refused to do next. Rather than declaring victory with injectable tirzepatide, management pressed forward on two parallel fronts: oral small-molecule GLP-1 therapy and triple-receptor agonism. On April 1, 2026, the FDA approved Foundayo (orforglipron), the first oral non-peptide GLP-1 agonist for chronic weight management that patients can take without food or water timing restrictions. Simultaneously, Lilly's triple agonist retatrutide (targeting GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon) delivered Phase 3 TRIUMPH weight-loss results approaching 28%, setting up a Q1 2027 regulatory filing. As Dave Ricks has emphasized in investor briefings, oral convenience and next-generation efficacy are how you turn a product cycle into a multi-decade platform.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Self-Cannibalization Is Lilly's Best Insurance Policy
callouts.text: When you and I examine pharmaceutical compounders, the fatal flaw is almost always hubris at the peak—defending an aging cash cow until generics or a rival's superior molecule arrives. By launching Foundayo in 2026 and advancing retatrutide toward 2027 while Mounjaro and Zepbound are still accelerating, Lilly is actively building the bridge over its own 2036+ tirzepatide patent cliff a full decade in advance.

book_subsections.title: Why the Next Decade Will Test Lilly's Capital Discipline
paragraphs: Every great business cycle creates its own specific temptation. In 2011, Lilly's temptation was defensive mega-M&A; today, with $65.2 billion in FY2025 revenue and $91 billion to $92 billion guided for FY2026, the temptation is overconfidence—assuming that tirzepatide's dominance is permanent and that manufacturing capacity can never be overbuilt.

If you and I study Pfizer's 2006–2015 cycle—where Lipitor's $13 billion peak masked R&D decay and the $2.8 billion Exubera inhaled-insulin write-off—the lesson is crystal clear. Delivery convenience, payer economics, and next-generation clinical superiority matter long before a patent expires. By launching Foundayo in 2026 and advancing triple-agonist retatrutide toward a Q1 2027 filing while Mounjaro and Zepbound are still growing at 40%+ rates, Lilly is demonstrating that it remembers the pain of 2011–2014.

book_subsections.title: The Cultural Thread Across 150 Years
paragraphs: Walk through Lilly's headquarters in Indianapolis and you notice something unusual for a global pharmaceutical giant: the company has never moved its home city, never pursued a hostile takeover, and never abandoned its founding focus on complex chronic diseases. From 1923's Iletin to 1982's Humulin to 2022's Mounjaro, Lilly's greatest breakthroughs have always been iterative leaps built on decades of institutional memory in endocrinology.

That institutional patience is why Lilly could stomach a six-year revenue plateau from 2011 to 2017 without gutting its labs. When you and I evaluate management teams, the hardest thing to measure is how they behave when the cycle turns against them. Lilly's behavior during the 'YZ' patent cliff—protecting R&D, divesting non-core animal health, and licensing early-stage mechanisms like Chugai's orforglipron—is the clearest proof of its compounding culture.

book_subsections.title: What the 1923–2026 Arc Teaches Us About Timing
paragraphs: If you step back and look at the full arc from Colonel Eli Lilly's 1876 apothecary to 2026's incretin leader, one practical lesson stands out for long-term investors. Great pharmaceutical compounders rarely look obvious in the middle of a patent cliff, and they rarely look risk-free at the peak of a product cycle. Between 2011 and 2017, Lilly's sales flatlined while it quietly funded the chemistry that became tirzepatide. Between 2022 and 2026, it turned that chemistry into a $65 billion-plus revenue engine while simultaneously building Foundayo and retatrutide.

Our job in this dossier is not to fall in love with the story, nor to dismiss it out of fear of concentration. Our job is to separate the durable scientific and manufacturing engine from the cyclical noise, and that starts by mapping every pillar of what Lilly actually sells today.

book_subsections.title: Why the 2011–2014 Patent Cliff Forged Today's R&D Discipline
paragraphs: Most investors today know Eli Lilly as a trillion-dollar incretin juggernaut. Few remember how close the company came to strategic drift between 2011 and 2014, when Zyprexa, Cymbalta, and Evista lost U.S. patent protection in rapid succession. Revenue fell from $24.3 billion in 2011 to $19.6 billion in 2014, forcing Lilly to cut costs while refusing to slash core R&D.

Instead of chasing a defensive mega-merger like several peers, Lilly doubled down on internal biologics and metabolic chemistry. That patience produced Trulicity in 2014, Taltz in 2016, Verzenio in 2017, and ultimately tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) in 2022–2023. Understanding that history explains why management still reinvests heavily into oral small molecules like Foundayo and triple agonists like retatrutide years before tirzepatide's 2036 patent expiry.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The 150-Year Pattern
book_callouts.text: History does not repeat verbatim in biopharma, but the structural pattern at Lilly is unmistakable: every durable expansion in its 150-year history—from Iletin in 1923 to Humulin in 1982 to tirzepatide and Foundayo in the 2020s—has paired novel molecular engineering with difficult-to-copy manufacturing scale.
